newsitem.title: USA: European-American elite gather in U.S. South.
newsitem.headline: European-American elite gather in U.S. South.

text.p: What do Henry Kissinger, Queen Beatrix of the Netherlands, Colin Powell, David Rockefeller and IBM Chairman Louis Gerstner have in common?
They are among 120 dignitaries from Europe and the United States meeting at a secluded Georgia island-lake resort as part of a semisecret organisation called the Bilderberg Group.
For four days beginning on Thursday, the group's influential guests are to be part of an informal think tank on world issues.

The Bilderberg Group was formed in the war-ravaged Europe of the early 1950s in reaction to a growing Communist threat. But in recent years, its secrecy and the influence wielded by its members have spawned a host of right-wing conspiracy theorists who see the organisation as the agent of a new world order.
The names of European royalty, executives of blue-chip corporations, economists, central bankers, journalists and heads of state appear on a roster of participants obtained by Reuters.

Listed as the Clinton administration's representative this year is Sandy Berger, assistant to the president for national security affairs. Former White House senior aide George Stephanopoulos is also expected to attend.
But the identities of invited dignitaries is about the only thing likely to be known for sure about the meeting.
The Bilderberg Group said in a statement that attendees had agreed not to be interviewed and added that there would be no news conference on Sunday when the meeting comes to an end.

The group is meeting behind several layers of security. Yet Georgia police this week confessed to having only a vague idea of the get-together, held on a state-owned island in Lake Lanier, 55 miles (95 km) northeast of Atlanta.
"We recently became aware of this meeting," spokesman John Bankhead of the Georgia Bureau of Investigation said tersely.
It was 1957 when the group last met in the state of Georgia. Last year the Bilderbergs met in Toronto.
But the first such meeting of Americans and Europeans took place in 1954 at the Bilderberg Hotel in Oosterbeck in the Netherlands, whose Prince Bernhard chaired it.

According to the Washington-based Liberty Lobby, which monitors Bilderberg activities, those who take part in the annual meetings are asked not to reveal the contents of their free and frank discussions. There are no votes, and no resolutions are passed.
"They will conduct the world's business behind locked and guarded doors," Jim Tucker, a reporter for a Liberty Lobby publication called The Spotlight, said.
